question: Why is a Dental Panoramic Tomograph (DPT) so called?
options: It shows a wide view of the slice containing the jaws
It shows a series of separate images of each tooth in turn
It is taken with the receptor inside the mouth
It shows the whole skull from a lateral view
explanation: A tomograph is an image of a 'slice' of the patient, and a DPT shows a wide view (panorama) of the slice containing the jaws.
extraWrong: It is taken with the patient lying down
It shows a cross-section of a single tooth
It shows only the temporomandibular joints

question: A tomograph is an image of a 'slice' of the patient.
explanation: A tomograph images a slice of the patient; the DPT shows a panorama of the slice containing the jaws.

question: During a panoramic exposure, how do the X-ray tubehead and the film or sensor move?
options: Both pass around the front of the face
The tubehead passes behind the head; the receptor passes in front of the face
The tubehead passes in front of the face; the receptor passes behind the head
Both stay still while the patient rotates
explanation: The receptor passes around the front of the face while the tubehead passes around the back of the head.
extraWrong: Both pass around the back of the head
The receptor stays still while the tubehead circles
The tubehead stays still while the receptor circles

question: What happens to structures lying outside the horseshoe-shaped focal trough on a panoramic image?
options: They are in focus and slightly magnified
They are in focus but slightly reduced in size
They appear blurred and distorted in size
They do not appear on the image at all
explanation: Structures outside the focal trough appear blurred and distorted in size; those within it are in focus and slightly magnified.
extraWrong: They are shown sharply at true size
They appear sharper than those inside it
They are always reduced to half size

question: In panoramic radiography, the X-ray beam is a horizontal slit angled downwards.
explanation: The beam is a vertical slit angled upwards at about eight degrees.

question: When taking a panoramic radiograph of an edentulous patient, what should be done?
options: Use the bite-peg and ask the patient to close the lips
Use the bite-peg supported with cotton wool rolls
Remove the chin support and centre the light on the nose
Omit the bite-peg and rest the chin on the chin support
explanation: For edentulous patients, do not use the bite-peg, rest the chin on the chin support and centre the canine light on the corner of the mouth.
extraWrong: Use the bite-peg and centre the light on the chin
Tilt the head back with the bite-peg in place
Keep the dentures in and use the bite-peg

question: For an edentulous patient having a panoramic radiograph, where should the canine positioning light beam be centred?
options: On the corner of the mouth
On the tip of the nose
On the lower border of the mandible
On the ala of the nose
explanation: The canine positioning light beam should be centred on the corner of the mouth for edentulous patients.
extraWrong: On the centre of the upper lip
On the point of the chin
On the tragus of the ear

question: For edentulous patients having a panoramic radiograph, the bite-peg should not be used.
explanation: The bite-peg is not used; the chin rests on the chin support instead.

question: What do TMJ programmes on panoramic equipment allow?
options: Only pre-selected parts of the patient to be exposed and captured
The condyles to be imaged with the mouth closed and open
The teeth to be imaged without a bite-peg
A test exposure to show machine movement
explanation: TMJ programmes enable the condyles to be imaged with the mouth closed and with the mouth open.
extraWrong: Children under six to be imaged safely
The beam to be angled downwards
Structures outside the focal trough to be in focus

question: Which of these is a clinical indication for a panoramic radiograph?
options: Routine caries diagnosis of the approximal contact areas
Root canal identification during endodontics
Assessment of third molars before planned surgery
Imaging a single incisor apex after trauma
explanation: Assessment of third molars prior to planned surgical intervention is a listed indication for panoramic tomography.
extraWrong: Checking for caries in a single premolar
Routine screening of every new patient
Monitoring a root filling on one tooth

question: Panoramic radiographs are not suitable for children under ten years of age.
explanation: They are not suitable for children under six years of age.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of dental panoramic tomographs?
options: Structures outside the focal trough are always clearly shown
No ghost or air shadows overlie the teeth
Equipment movement improves image quality
Can be taken even if the patient cannot open their mouth
explanation: A large area is imaged on one image even if the patient cannot open their mouth, which is useful following trauma.
extraWrong: Every structure is shown at its true size
It is suitable for children under six
Equipment movement never affects quality

question: On an ideal panoramic radiograph, where should the image of the hard palate appear?
options: Above the apices of the upper teeth
Over the roots of the upper teeth
Below the crowns of the lower teeth
Level with the occlusal plane
explanation: The hard palate should appear above the apices of the upper teeth.
extraWrong: Below the apices of the lower teeth
Across the crowns of the upper teeth
Over the condyles of the mandible

question: On a panoramic radiograph, what does an air shadow above the tongue create?
options: A radiopaque (white) band over the lower incisor crowns
A radiolucent band over the roots of the upper teeth
A ghost shadow of the cervical spine
A blurred image of the condyles
explanation: An air shadow above the tongue creates a radiolucent (black) band over the roots of the upper teeth, so density is not uniform.
extraWrong: A radiopaque band along the lower border of the mandible
A double image of the hard palate
A ghost shadow of an earring

question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of dental panoramic tomographs?
options: Patient positioning is very complicated
It is a relatively high-dose examination for the patient
Some patients' jaws do not fit the shape of the focal trough
It cannot be used with solid-state digital sensor technology
explanation: Some patients' jaw shapes do not conform to the focal trough; panoramics are otherwise relatively simple to position, low-dose and compatible with solid-state technology.
extraWrong: It cannot be taken if the patient cannot open the mouth
It is a poor teaching aid for patients
Field limitation techniques are not available

question: On an ideal panoramic radiograph, the right and left molar teeth should be equal in mesio-distal dimension.
explanation: Equal mesio-distal size of the right and left molars is an ideal image quality criterion, alongside equal vertical and horizontal magnification.

question: In panoramic radiography, the vertical slit X-ray beam is angled upwards at approximately what angle?
options: About 30 degrees
About 8 degrees
About 45 degrees
About 60 degrees
explanation: The panoramic X-ray beam is a vertical slit angled upwards at about 8 degrees.
extraWrong: About 20 degrees
About 75 degrees
About 90 degrees

question: What do field limitation techniques on panoramic equipment allow?
options: The condyles to be imaged with the mouth open and closed
Edentulous patients to be imaged without a bite-peg
Children under six to be imaged
Only pre-selected parts of the patient to be exposed and captured
explanation: Field limitation techniques mean only pre-selected parts of the patient are exposed and captured on the final image.
extraWrong: Structures outside the focal trough to be in focus
A test exposure to show the machine movement
The patient to rotate instead of the machine

question: When preparing a patient for a panoramic radiograph, what can be used, if necessary, to show them how the machine moves?
options: A field limitation programme
The canine positioning light
A test exposure
A TMJ programme
explanation: The procedure and equipment are explained and, if necessary, a test exposure is used to show the machine movement.
extraWrong: A protective lead apron
The bite-peg
A cotton wool roll

question: On a panoramic radiograph, patient movement in the vertical plane distorts only the part of the image being produced at that instant.
explanation: This is listed as an advantage of panoramic tomography: vertical movement only distorts the part of the image being produced at that moment.

question: In panoramic radiographs, how would teeth appear if they are outside of the horseshoe focal trough?
options: Blurry
Sharp & clear
Small
explanation: If the patient is positioned correctly the teeth will appear clear, sharp & slightly magnified. If the patient's head is too far back, the lower teeth will appear magnified but blurry.

question: The thin radiolucent lines either side of a panoramic x-ray are the inferior dental canals?
explanation: Edges of the canals are radiopaque & well-defined as you're looking at them edge on.

question: How might you modify the technique to take a panoramic radiograph on an edentulous patient?
options: Aim canine positioning light at the corner of the mouth
Position patient further forward to ensure sharp image of anterior maxilla
Lower chin rest so patient's spine is curved
Instruct patient's tongue is firmly pressed to floor of their mouth
explanation: Can't use bite peg.

question: On a dental panoramic radiograph, how do objects inside the horseshoe shaped focal trough appear?
options: Magnified
Intensified
Ionised
Minimised
explanation: Sensor is far away from patient's face - the image 'spreads out' as it passes the gap, so image grows. Think: horse is big if inside your kitchen.

question: Which of the following is NOT a clinical indication for taking a panoramic radiograph?
options: Routine screening
Grossly neglected mouth
Mandibular fractures
Pre-implant planning
explanation: Each radiograph taken must be justified according to clinical need.

question: Which of the following is an advantage of dental panoramic radiographs?
options: Can be used even if patient can't open their mouth (following trauma)
Soft tissue shadows, ghost or air shadows can overlie important hard tissue structures
Shape of jaws may not conform to shape of focus or focal trough
Structures or abnormalities not in focal trough may not be evident
explanation: All tissues within the in-focus layer are shown on one image even if the patient cannot open their mouth, which is useful following trauma; B, C and D are disadvantages.

question: Which of the following is the most accurate description of a dental panoramic radiograph?
options: 3D representation of teeth + jaws
General overview of patient's maxillofacial skeleton
Slice of the patient showing teeth & jaws
Type of computed tomograph or CT scan
explanation: While it is a tomograph, it's not built by computer like a CT or CBCT.
